The mist clings to the reeds this morning. It will lift when it pleases.
A stranger's steps sound different on the dock. Yours are soft enough.
The pond is flat as a skipped stone today. Fish sleep in, I think.
My old bones say rain by evening. The heron agrees. He always does.
You have the look of someone who listens. That is rarer than a big catch.
Bait sits in the tin, patient as a stone. It knows its moment will come.
A slow tide teaches the best knots. Mine are slow indeed.
The heron and I share this shore. He takes the fish. I take the quiet.
Morning is a borrowed thing. Best returned with a full creel.
Your greeting was short and kind. That is how I like my tea, too.
The water holds the sky upside down. Some days I prefer it that way.
An old boat drifts where the wind says. So do old men, given time.
Fish do not know my name. They know my shadow. Close enough.
The dock creaks a welcome. Heh. It does that for everyone.
You stand still as a heron. That is a fine way to begin.
A tangled line is just a lesson in disguise. I have many lessons.
The mist tastes like morning and old wood smoke. Familiar.
My net dries on the fence. It dreams of deeper water. So do I.
Speak low near the pond. The fish are gossips. So are the gulls.
A quiet greeting is worth two loud ones. You knew that already.
The sun warms the planks but not the water. That comes later.
You do not fidget. I notice such things. Most folks fidget.
An empty hook still teaches the hand. Mine learned long ago.
The tide is neither early nor late. It is simply the tide.
My cat left a fish tail on the doorstep. A gift, I think. Heh.
The reeds whisper when the wind shifts. They are saying nothing.
You walk like the path owes you no favors. I respect that.
A fisherman's welcome is a nod and a dry spot. Consider both given.
The heron just blinked at me. Slow as a Sunday. I blinked back.
Rain will come when the frogs start. They are quiet still.
The pond keeps its fish and its counsel. Both are deep.
I mended the fence this morning. The fish did not notice. Typical.
Your shadow falls on the water. The minnows scatter. No harm done.
An old proverb says greet the day before it greets you. Heh. I made that up.
The kettle is cold now but the company is warm. Sit anyway.
You came down the hill slow. That is the right speed for this place.
The tide pools hold tiny worlds. I check them most mornings.
My oars rest against the shed. They are as tired as I am.
A fish jumped at dawn and startled the heron. He glared at me.
The village is quiet this hour. Even the dogs are dreaming.
You have mud on your boots. Good. The path here is honest mud.
The wind smells of rain and far water. It will pass or it will not.
A slow hand on the line feels every tug. That is the whole art.
The heron stands on one leg for hours. I have tried. My knee complained.
Morning light makes the pond look shallow. It is not. Nothing is.
You greeted me without wanting anything. That is a fine quality.
The old cat follows you with his eyes. He does that to the worthy.
A fisherman waits for the tide, not the clock. The clock is wrong often.
The reeds are green and the water is gray. A good combination.
My boots are wet through again. The pond is generous that way.
You do not ask where the fish are. That is a good start.
The heron just stole a minnow. Tiny theft. Tiny criminal. Heh.
The dock has a loose board near the end. Step wide or step slow.
A proverb says a quiet guest brings good weather. I just made that up.
The mist is burning off the far shore. The day is deciding.
You look like you have walked a long road. Rest here a moment.
Fish rise when they please. So do I. We are alike that way.
The village has one bell and it is cracked. We like it that way.
My hands are cold but the line is patient. So is the pond.
The heron is preening like he owns the place. He might, by now.
